analysis.one_liner: Makes public community college tuition-free and covers tuition at public four-year colleges for working- and middle-class students.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 21, 2025 with 75 Democratic cosponsors; referred to three House committees and has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a federal-state partnership that pays to wipe out tuition and required fees for every student at public community colleges and for working- and middle-class students at public four-year colleges — up to $150,000 of income for a single student or parent, $300,000 for a married couple [S2][S3]. It roughly doubles the maximum Pell Grant at public and tribal schools, lets students use Pell for living costs, extends Pell eligibility to Dreamer students, and funds tuition elimination at private nonprofit historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions [S2][S3]. It also requires participating states to keep funding higher education at current levels and to hire more full-time, tenure-track faculty [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Students at community colleges (tuition eliminated for all), working- and middle-class students at public four-year colleges (household income up to $150,000 single / $300,000 married), Pell recipients (maximum award raised to $14,790 at public and tribal schools, usable for living expenses, duration extended to 7.5 years), Dreamer and other immigrant students newly made eligible for aid, students at private nonprofit HBCUs and minority-serving institutions, and low-income and first-generation students supported by TRIO and GEAR UP programs [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Community college and public university students

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates tuition and required fees for all eligible students at community colleges and two-year tribal colleges, starting with award year 2026-2027 [S2][S3].

Eliminates tuition and fees for working- and middle-class students at public four-year institutions — up to $150,000 adjusted gross income for a single parent or independent student, $300,000 for married parents or a married independent student [S3].

Raises the maximum Pell Grant to $14,790 for students at public and tribal institutions, allows Pell to be used for living and non-tuition expenses, and extends the eligibility window from 12 semesters to 7.5 years [S3].
Extends Pell Grant and federal aid eligibility to Dreamer students and students with DACA, temporary protected status, or deferred enforced departure status [S2][S3].

Funds tuition elimination at private nonprofit historically Black colleges and universities and minority-serving institutions, and reauthorizes TRIO through FY2035 and GEAR UP through FY2029 [S2][S3].

Requires participating states to maintain per-student funding at recent average levels, cap out-of-state charges near marginal cost, meet a staffing ratio for disability services, and ensure at least 75% of instruction is delivered by tenure-track or tenured faculty within five years [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through direct appropriations of unspecified 'such sums as may be necessary' each year through FY2035, with a federal share starting at $5,110 per community college student and $11,610 per four-year public college student. Participating states must contribute a growing state share (0% rising to 20% by 2030-31) and cannot cut per-student higher education spending below recent three-year averages [S3].

drawbacks.text: The cost is enormous and open-ended: the bill directly appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' through FY2035 with no revenue source or spending offset, which is the central objection an honest supporter must acknowledge [S3].

The income thresholds are generous — a married couple earning up to $300,000 would pay no tuition at public four-year schools — so critics argue a large share of the benefit goes to families that could pay [S3].

Participating states must sustain or raise higher education funding and eventually cover 20% of costs, and institutions are barred from using grant funds for administration, capital projects, or athletics, which some states and universities would find burdensome [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — tuition-free access to community college for everyone and near-universal affordability at public four-year schools, plus a much larger Pell Grant covering living costs — is large and durable. The cost is also large and, as written, not paid for by any offset in the bill; whether the trade is worth it depends on views about federal borrowing and priorities. The design includes real guardrails (state maintenance-of-effort, tenure-track hiring requirements, tuition caps on remaining charges) that aim to keep the money from being absorbed by price increases.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, and none of them has taken it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it simply sits.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the College for All Act of 2025 in the House on May 21, 2025 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the Committees on Education and Workforce, Ways and Means, and Budget [S5].
The full action history shows no activity after that referral — no hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred [S5].
All 75 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the outcome simply preserves the status quo: tuition stays where it is, which is most convenient for the institutions and lenders whose federal-aid revenue a tuition-free public system would have displaced. No new spending obligation was created either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; status quo preserved

sides.party_line_note: All 75 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a progressive Democrat; no Republican has signed on, and Republicans hold the House majority that controls committee agendas and floor time.

industries.note: The bill creates a permanent federal funding stream that pays most of the cost of tuition elimination at public two- and four-year schools, locking in federal support for public higher education while attaching real rules: state maintenance-of-effort, tenure-track hiring minimums, tuition caps, and bans on spending grant funds on administration or athletics. Students get free tuition; the institutions get guaranteed revenue.

The bill routes federal dollars to public, tribal, HBCU, and minority-serving institutions and excludes for-profit schools, while counting state aid to proprietary institutions against nothing in the maintenance-of-effort formula — shrinking their competitive position against a free public alternative.

With tuition eliminated for most public-college students and Pell expanded to cover living costs, students would need to borrow substantially less, shrinking the market for federal and private student loans over time.

industries.industry: Private nonprofit four-year colleges (other than HBCUs and minority-serving institutions)
industries.note: They receive no grant funding under the bill and could lose enrollment to tuition-free public options, though the bill does not bar their students from existing Pell aid and some students would still choose them.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans controlling the House and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or a vote in this Congress. Its realistic path is to expire at the end of the 119th Congress in January 2027 while serving as a template and messaging vehicle for future free-college proposals.
